section.title: An Invitation to the Thirsty
section.sectionRationale: Fresh from the Servant's atoning death and Zion's promised fruitfulness, Isaiah opens the widest door in the whole book: come, everyone who thirsts, come, buy without money. It is the natural next word after chapter 53, the invitation that flows from a finished, costly atonement, offered free to all who will come.
section.thesis: Because the Servant's suffering has secured salvation, God now issues an open, urgent invitation to everyone who thirsts to come without money and be satisfied, to seek Him while He may be found, and to trust that His word, once sent out, will not return empty but will accomplish everything He intends.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the free invitation to eat and drink; the call to seek the LORD and return to Him, since His thoughts are not our thoughts; and the sure, fruitful power of God's word, sending His people out with joy.

units.label: Come, all you who are thirsty
units.note: buy without money and without cost

verses.text: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!
Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy? Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in the richest of foods.
Incline your ear and come to Me; listen, so that your soul may live. I will make with you an everlasting covenant, My {{chesedDavid|loving devotion}} promised to David.
Behold, I have made him a witness to the nations, a leader and commander of the peoples.
Surely you will summon a nation you do not know, and nations who do not know you will run to you. For the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, has bestowed glory on you.”

units.label: Seek the LORD while He may be found
units.note: His thoughts are not our thoughts

verses.text: Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near.
Let the wicked man forsake his own way and the unrighteous man his own thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion, and to our God, for He will freely pardon.
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways,” declares the LORD.
“For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts.

units.label: My word will not return empty

verses.text: For just as rain and snow fall from heaven and do not return without watering the earth, making it bud and sprout, and providing seed to sow and food to eat,
so My {{dabar|word}} that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please, and it will prosper where I send it.
You will indeed go out with joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and hills will burst into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands.
Instead of the thornbush, a cypress will grow, and instead of the brier, a myrtle will spring up; they will make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign, never to be destroyed.”

chesedDavid.gloss: The loving devotion, or sure mercies, promised to David, referring to God's covenant faithfulness to David's line in 2 Samuel 7. Paul quotes this exact phrase in Acts 13:34 as proof that Jesus, raised from the dead, is the fulfillment of that everlasting Davidic promise.

dabar.gloss: Word, spoken utterance with inherent power to act. God's dabar does not merely describe reality, it accomplishes it, the same creative word that spoke light into being in Genesis 1 and that John identifies as the eternal Word who became flesh, John 1:1, 14.

basic.context: Right after the Suffering Servant's atonement and Zion's promised fruitfulness, Isaiah throws open an invitation to everyone who thirsts, no money required, to come and be satisfied. It reads like the natural next word once the cost of salvation has already been paid by another.
basic.hermeneutics: This is gospel invitation in Old Testament dress, urgent, universal in its call though answered by those who actually come, and grounded not in human effort, buy without money, but in God's initiative and provision. The chapter also confronts the difference between God's ways and ours, and promises that His spoken word never fails to accomplish its purpose.
basic.originalLanguages: God's chasdei David, the sure loving devotion promised to David, becomes, in Acts 13:34, Paul's proof text that the resurrection of Jesus fulfills God's everlasting covenant with David's line. And God's dabar, word, is pictured as rain and snow, never returning empty, always accomplishing what it is sent to do.
basic.typology: The free invitation to water, bread, wine, and milk without cost anticipates Jesus' own invitation, if anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink, John 7:37, and the free gift of the water of life in Revelation 22:17. The everlasting covenant and mercies of David point directly to Christ, David's greater Son.
basic.christ: Jesus stands in the temple and echoes this very chapter, if anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink, John 7:37, offering Himself as the fulfillment of Isaiah's free invitation. Paul, in his first recorded sermon, quotes Isaiah 55:3 to prove that Jesus' resurrection fulfills the sure, everlasting mercies promised to David, Acts 13:34.
basic.god: God is not a reluctant seller extracting payment, He is a Host who has already paid the cost and now simply calls the thirsty to come and receive freely. His ways are higher than ours precisely in this: where we calculate what people deserve, He freely pardons all who return to Him.
basic.crossReferences: John 7:37 has Jesus issue the same invitation to the thirsty at the Feast of Tabernacles. Acts 13:34 quotes 55:3 of Christ's resurrection fulfilling David's sure mercies. Revelation 22:17 closes the whole Bible with the same free invitation, let the one who is thirsty come.
basic.oneStory: From a costly, finished atonement flows a free, urgent invitation: come, thirsty ones, without money, and be satisfied. That invitation runs through Jesus' own words at the temple and through the last page of Revelation, because the whole Bible's story ends exactly where Isaiah 55 begins, an open door to anyone who will come.

context.literary:
Isaiah 55 is the last chapter of the long section that began at Isaiah 40, and it is written to be heard against that beginning. The section opened with 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1, and with the promise that 'the word of our God stands forever,' Isaiah 40:8. It closes with the word that goes out and does not return empty, verse 11. The whole book of consolation is bracketed by the speaking God.

Inside that frame the poem moves in three waves. Verses 1 to 5 are a run of imperatives, come, buy, eat, listen, incline, come, in the voice of a market trader, and they end with a promise addressed to a people. Verses 6 and 7 turn the same urgency toward repentance. Verses 8 to 13 then pile up the grounds for confidence, and the English 'For' that opens verses 8, 9 and 10 marks each one as a reason: God's thoughts are higher, His ways are higher, and His word is like the rain.

A quiet device joins the last two sections. In verse 11 the word 'proceeds' from God's mouth, and in verse 12 the people 'go out' with joy. The same Hebrew verb, yatsa, is behind both. The word goes out, and so do the people it was sent to rescue.

The chapter also answers the chapter before it. Isaiah 54 ends by speaking of the 'servants of the LORD' in the plural, Isaiah 54:17, the family promised to the suffering Servant in Isaiah 53:10. Chapter 55 turns to that family and tells them what is on the table. The poem then closes the book of consolation with a picture of creation itself joining the celebration, as the mountains sing and the trees clap, verse 12.
context.historical:
The first hearers were people whose world had shrunk. The kingdom of Judah had fallen, the temple lay in ruins, and the Davidic king had been carried to Babylon. His last glimpse in the history books is of Jehoiachin eating at a foreign king's table on a daily allowance, 2 Kings 25:27-30. Many of the exiles had settled and done well enough. Babylon offered work, markets and a measure of comfort.

That is the setting for a question that sounds odd until it is heard there: 'Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?' verse 2. The prophet is not scolding the poor. He is asking a settled people whether the life they are building in a foreign empire is the thing that can actually feed them, when the God who promised to bring them home is calling.

The images are ordinary ones of the ancient Near East. Water was precious and had to be fetched or bought, and wine and milk were the foods of feasts and weddings, as in Song of Songs 5:1. An invitation to drink and eat 'without money' is an invitation to a banquet someone else has paid for.

Verses 12 and 13 use the language of the exodus. A people 'led forth in peace' echoes Isaiah 52:12, where Israel will not leave in haste because the LORD goes before them. The story of the return was not a mere hope. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia issued a decree that sent the exiles home, Ezra 1:1-4, a king Isaiah had named long before, Isaiah 44:28. The prophet's word was, in the plainest sense, about to be tested.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on older Scripture and is drawn on in turn. Wisdom had already set a table in Proverbs 9:1-6, calling the simple to eat her bread and drink her wine, and the psalms had given thirst a voice, 'My soul thirsts for God, the living God,' Psalm 42:2. Jeremiah had diagnosed the reason people turn away from the fountain, digging 'broken cisterns that cannot hold water,' Jeremiah 2:13. Isaiah 55:2 reads like the same charge turned into a question.

Behind verse 3 stands the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, the promise of an offspring and an enduring throne, which the psalms celebrate, Psalm 89:28-29. Verse 13 reverses Genesis 3:18, where the ground yielded thorns and thistles. The rest of the prophets keep adding to the picture of this new covenant, Isaiah 61:8, Jeremiah 32:40 and Ezekiel 37:26, each calling it everlasting.

The New Testament takes the chapter up at the points where Jesus speaks of thirst and bread. He cries out in the temple, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, and tells a Samaritan woman about water that becomes a spring, John 4:13-14. Paul quotes verse 3 to prove that God raised Jesus never to see decay, Acts 13:34. The Bible's last invitation, Revelation 22:17, and the promise to the thirsty in Revelation 21:6, take their shape from this chapter, and both end with the offer of the water of life 'freely'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wanted a discouraged, half-settled people to believe three things at once. First, that the God who had promised them a return was not bargaining with them but giving. The language of buying without money is a deliberate shock, because everything they knew about food and water ran on payment. Second, that the promises made to David had not died with the monarchy. Verse 3 says 'I will make with you,' and the pronoun is plural. The covenant that once belonged to a royal house is now offered to the whole community, and the role of the king as a witness to the nations, verse 4, passes to a people who will 'summon a nation you do not know,' verse 5.

Third, he wanted them to trust a word that sounded improbable. The idea that the exiles of a defeated nation would walk home with the hills singing was hard to credit, and verses 8 to 11 are an argument from the character of God, not from the circumstances. The people were meant to answer the invitation by turning, verse 7, and to rest on the promise that what God has said will happen. The poem is warm but it is not casual. It tells people what to do with the time they have.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the chapter is a direct address, and the commands are meant to be obeyed: come, listen, seek, call, forsake, return. They are not in tension with the idea that the gift is free. Coming and listening are the empty hand that receives, not the payment that earns. The words 'without money and without cost' are about the gift, while 'forsake' and 'return' in verse 7 describe how a person actually receives it. Treating the free offer as permission to stay where we are would miss the second half of the sentence.

Two things are descriptive rather than prescriptive. The picture of mountains breaking into song and trees clapping, verse 12, is poetry about the joy of a renewed world, not a rule for worship or a claim about trees. And verse 11 describes what God's word does, not what every preacher's words will do. It promises that what God has purposed will be accomplished, not that each sermon will visibly succeed. It also does not teach that people may sit and wait for God to act without turning, since the invitation is the very word that does the work.

debates.question: Who holds the promise to David in verses 3 to 5?

views.label: The people of God as a community
views.case: The pronoun in verse 3 is plural and the covenant is made 'with you.' On this view the royal promises, once tied to the house of David, are shared out to the exiles as a whole, so that Israel itself becomes the witness who draws the nations in verse 5. Isaiah 54:17 has just given 'the servants of the LORD' their inheritance, which fits the plural turn.

views.label: A coming Davidic king
views.case: The 'him' of verse 4 is a single figure who is 'a witness to the nations, a leader and commander of the peoples,' and that sounds like the promised descendant of 2 Samuel 7:12-16. The people receive the benefits of a covenant that is carried by the king, much as the exiles in Isaiah 42:6 receive light through one appointed as a covenant for the people.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Paul's use in Acts 13:34 treats the sure blessings as given to a people through the risen Son of David. The community holds the promise because the king does, so the plural and singular belong to one covenant.

debates.bearing: The third reading does justice to the grammar of both verses and to Paul's argument. The people are invited to take what is theirs because a King has taken it for them.

debates.question: What does 'while He may be found' in verse 6 mean?

views.label: A real window that will close
views.case: The urgency is literal. The exiles had a particular opportunity, with Cyrus's decree and the road home, and later Scripture warns that the opportunity of 'today' does not last, Hebrews 3:13. On this view there is a day when seeking comes too late, as in Amos 8:11, with its famine of hearing the words of the LORD.

views.label: A call to respond now, not a threat that God will withdraw
views.case: God describes Himself elsewhere as found by those who never asked for Him, Isaiah 65:1, and promises that those who search with all their heart will find, Jeremiah 29:13. The urgency here is an appeal to people who tend to postpone, not a statement about God's availability.

debates.bearing: Both are true to Scripture's balance. The door is open and God is not hiding, but delay is a danger to the one who delays, since hearts harden, and so the right response is to come today.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 opens with a small word that carries a lot. The Hebrew hoy, translated 'come' in the BSB, is usually the cry of woe in the prophets, as in Isaiah 5:8 and 5:11. Here it is used as a call, the trader's 'Ho there!' in the street. The same word that so often announces judgment now announces a feast, and it makes the listener stop. The chapter's first sound is an attention-getting cry, not a sermon.

The covenant in verse 3 is literally one that God will 'cut,' the ordinary Hebrew way of speaking of making a covenant, from the practice of cutting a sacrifice. The covenant is described as 'everlasting,' berit olam, a phrase used of the covenants with Noah, Abraham and David, and promised again in Isaiah 61:8 and Jeremiah 32:40. The 'loving devotion' in this verse is plural in Hebrew, the faithful acts of loyalty promised to David, and the word that follows them means sure or reliable, from the same root as 'amen.' When Paul quotes the verse in Acts 13:34, he uses the Greek Septuagint rendering, which speaks of the hosia, the holy things, of David that are pista, faithful. The Greek chooses a word for what is holy and trustworthy, and Paul places it beside the resurrection.

Verse 7 ends with one of the most generous phrases in the Old Testament. God 'will freely pardon' renders a Hebrew construction that says He will multiply to pardon, yarbeh lislo'ach, as though pardon were something He supplies in quantity. The verb salach, to forgive, has God as its subject in the Old Testament, so pardon is always seen as His to give. The compassion God promises in the same verse comes from a root related to the word for the womb, and carries the sense of a mother's tenderness.

Verse 11 holds a pair of words worth setting side by side. The word 'proceeds' and the people 'go out' in verse 12 are the same verb. The word that 'will not return to Me empty,' reqam, is a word for emptiness and failure, and it is set against what God 'pleases,' hephets, His desire or purpose, and what the word 'will prosper,' from the root tsalach. God's speech is described as a messenger sent with a task and a delight to carry out.

Finally, verse 13 says the new growth will be 'an everlasting sign,' ot olam. Ot is the word for the covenant signs, the rainbow, circumcision and the Sabbath, Genesis 9:12, Genesis 17:11 and Exodus 31:13. The rebuilt landscape becomes a sign of the covenant itself. The word translated 'instead of,' tachat, begins both halves of the verse, and the Hebrew names of the thorny plants are not the thorns and thistles of Genesis 3:18. So the link to the curse is by theme and not by shared vocabulary, which is why it should be stated as an echo and not as a quotation.

typology.type: Water, wine and milk without money, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's market is a picture of what only God can supply, and Jesus steps into it. On the last day of the feast He stands and calls the thirsty to come to Him, John 7:37-38, and tells the woman at the well that He gives water that becomes a spring in the one who drinks, John 4:13-14. In the Bible's last chapter the same invitation is given by the Spirit and the bride, Revelation 22:17. The escalation is that Isaiah points to a gift and Jesus says the gift is found in Him, Isaiah's water becoming the Giver. The type falls short because ordinary water quenches thirst for an hour, while He gives what lasts.

typology.type: The everlasting covenant, the sure blessings of David, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The promise of an enduring throne in 2 Samuel 7:16 looked for a son who would not die. David's tomb was still in Jerusalem, as Peter observes, Acts 2:29, so the promise needed someone who would leave the grave. Paul sees it fulfilled in the resurrection, Acts 13:34, and Romans 1:3-4 says Jesus was declared Son of God in power by His resurrection from the dead, as a descendant of David. The correspondence is that a king's promise is kept by a risen King. The type falls short because every human son of David died; only this one lives to hold the throne.

typology.type: The word that goes out and does not return empty, verses 10 and 11
typology.fulfillment: The rain that falls and brings seed and bread is a picture of the word that God sends. John opens his Gospel with the Word who was with God and became flesh, John 1:1 and 1:14, and the pattern of Isaiah 55 fits Him closely. He came down from heaven and, near the end, said He had accomplished the work He was given, John 17:4. He also said a kernel of wheat that falls to the ground and dies bears much fruit, John 12:24, which is the rain-to-seed-to-bread movement in a single image. This is an echo and not a stated quotation. The type falls short because in Isaiah the word is spoken, while in John the Word is a person.

typology.type: Thorns replaced by cypress and myrtle, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The curse on the ground in Genesis 3:18 brought thorns, and Isaiah promises a land where they give way to trees that stand for life. Paul says creation was subjected to futility in hope that it will be set free from its bondage to decay, Romans 8:20-21, and that freedom rests on Christ, who redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The climax is the city where there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:3. The type falls short because Isaiah's picture is of a landscape, and the New Testament shows that the cure of the land follows the cure of the people.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by invitation. Jesus does not point to a source of living water somewhere else. He stands up on the last and greatest day of the feast and says, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. Jews who knew Isaiah would have heard the voice of the trader in Isaiah 55:1 coming from a man. To a Samaritan woman He says that if she knew the gift of God and who was asking her for a drink, she would have asked Him, John 4:10. He calls Himself the bread of life, and says whoever comes to Him will never hunger or thirst, John 6:35. Isaiah asks what to do with money spent on 'that which is not bread,' and Jesus answers with Himself.

The invitation is free, but it is not cheap, and here the chapter has to be read with the one before it. Isaiah 53 says the LORD laid on His Servant the iniquity of us all, Isaiah 53:6, and that the Servant bore it, Isaiah 53:11. The words 'without money and without cost' are possible because someone else has paid. Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with 'the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. Paul says we are 'justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,' Romans 3:24. The gift is free to the hearer because it cost the Giver everything.

The chapter also leads to Christ by covenant. The sure blessings promised to David are carried by the risen Son of David. Peter, preaching at Pentecost, argues that David died and his tomb remains, but that he foresaw the resurrection of the Christ, Acts 2:29-31, and Paul, at Pisidian Antioch, ties the quotation of Isaiah 55:3 to the same resurrection, Acts 13:34-37. The throne that never ends, Luke 1:32-33, is the throne of the One who rose.

Verses 4 and 5 look forward to the nations. The one made 'a witness to the nations' is echoed by the 'faithful witness' of Revelation 1:5 and by the king who came 'to testify to the truth,' John 18:37. When Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, they quote Isaiah's call to be a light to the nations, Acts 13:47, and the nations that 'run to you' in verse 5 are the harvest of a Messiah who says all authority is His and sends His people to make disciples of every nation, Matthew 28:18-19.

One caution keeps the reading honest. The wine and the milk are not codes for particular sacraments, and the thorn and the cypress are not hidden persons. What the New Testament authorizes is the link between the invitation and Jesus, between the Davidic covenant and the resurrection, and between the word that goes out and the Word made flesh. He is also the one who answers the call to seek with His own seeking, for the Son of Man 'came to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all the one who speaks and who means what He says. The poem is made of His speech, and its climax says His word is as sure as rain. That is how the Bible introduces Him at the start, when 'He spoke, and it came to be,' Psalm 33:9, and how it describes the word that outlasts the withering of the grass, Isaiah 40:8. What He says He will do, He does. For the exiles this meant that a prophecy of return was not a hope but a forecast.

He is a God who gives in a way no seller does. Verse 1 makes that vivid, and the point of verse 2 is that the alternatives are expensive and empty. The Giver wants to feed people and does not ask for a price. He also takes the initiative twice over. He calls the thirsty, and He tells Israel that they will 'summon a nation you do not know,' verse 5, so that even the gathering of the nations is His work, done through His people. Those who respond have been summoned and then enabled.

Verses 8 and 9 are often read as a statement that God is beyond understanding. In the argument of the chapter they say something more specific. They follow the call to the wicked to forsake their way and return, and they explain why God will pardon so abundantly: His thoughts and ways are higher, as the heavens are above the earth, in this, that He forgives where people would not. The same contrast is made in Hosea 11:9, 'For I am God and not man,' where God declines to destroy because He is the Holy One in their midst. The holiness of God is shown in His mercy, not set against it.

He is the Lord of creation as well as of the heart. Rain and snow do their work under His hand, and mountains and trees join the praise. The picture is of a world that is not merely the backdrop for redemption but takes part in it. This is a God who intends not only to forgive people but to put right the ground that was cursed.

He is also near and accessible, and urgent about it. The commands to seek Him and call on Him presume that He can be found and that He is close, verse 6. Yet He is not at our disposal, for His thoughts are not ours.

For worship this means the right posture is that of empty hands. We come not to pay but to receive, we listen and we trust a word we cannot yet see fulfilled. We can sing, as the creation does, because the God who promised is the one who always completes what He sends His word to do.

crossReferences.note: Wisdom builds her house, sets her table and sends out her servants to call the simple to eat her bread and drink her wine. Isaiah 55 has the same shape of a feast offered on the street, and the call to leave folly and live matches the call to forsake our own way. The Lord's table is the same table seen from the other side.

God's charge is that His people forsook the fountain of living water and dug broken cisterns. Isaiah 55:2 puts the same complaint as a question about money and labor spent on what does not satisfy. Both prophets say the problem is not that people thirst, but that they drink from the wrong place.

The original promise to David of a descendant, a kingdom and a throne that will last forever, with loving devotion that will never be removed. Isaiah 55:3 takes this covenant, calls it everlasting, and makes it available to a people in exile, which shows that it had not been cancelled by the fall of the monarchy.

The chapter on the suffering Servant says He will see His offspring, see the light of life and be satisfied, and justify many. Isaiah 55 is the invitation to that offspring, the people He bought. It explains how the gift can be without cost: the cost has already been borne in chapter 53.

Paul uses Isaiah 55:3 in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch to argue that God has fulfilled His promises by raising Jesus, who did not see decay as David did. The 'holy and sure blessings promised to David' are shown to rest in the resurrection, so a verse about exiles becomes the ground of the gospel.

Jesus calls the thirsty to come to Him and drink, and the Gospel explains that He is speaking about the Spirit who would be given after He was glorified. The water of Isaiah 55:1 is therefore tied to the Spirit's coming, and the invitation to drink is an invitation to receive the life of God Himself.

The ground was cursed so that it yielded thorns and thistles. Isaiah 55:13 promises that in place of the thornbush and the brier, living trees will grow. The Hebrew words differ, so the link is one of theme, but it sets the future of the creation against its fall.

God says He was found by those who did not seek Him and said 'Here I am' to a nation that did not call His name. This balances Isaiah 55:6. The command to seek is real, but behind it is a God who seeks out people before they look for Him, which is why the invitation can be offered to the unworthy.

God declares He will not turn back to destroy Ephraim, for He is God and not man, the Holy One among them. The contrast between divine and human ways in Isaiah 55:8 is of the same kind: He is higher than us by being more merciful, not less.

The word of the LORD made the heavens, and when He spoke, it came to be. This is the power behind Isaiah 55:11. The word that creates the world by command is the word that goes out to accomplish what pleases Him, which is why it cannot return empty.

A famine is coming, 'not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD.' This is the opposite of Isaiah's feast. It shows that the real hunger is for the word, and that the offer to 'listen carefully' in Isaiah 55:2 matters because the word can be withdrawn.

The One on the throne says, 'To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.' The offer of Isaiah 55:1 is made at the end of history as well as the middle, and it is by the same word, freely, that the whole story comes to rest.

study.oneStory:
The first tree in the Bible came with a word of generosity: 'You may eat freely from every tree of the garden,' Genesis 2:16. Isaiah 55 is that generosity restored to people who learned by loss what it was to trade it for something smaller. In Eden a word was doubted and the table lost, and the result was thorns, toil and a long journey away from the presence of God. The chapter returns to that moment and speaks the gift again, in the context of an exile that is its last echo.

It also draws together several threads of the story. The covenant made with Abraham looked toward the blessing of the nations, and verse 5 renews that goal. The covenant with David had promised an enduring throne, and verse 3 promises it to a people who had lost their king. The exodus had shown God leading His people out in peace, and verse 12 uses that language for a new departure. Isaiah is not building something new. He is showing that all the older promises were one promise, ready to be given freely.

The story afterward is told by the gospel writers, who take the chapter's pictures of water, bread and a covenant that cannot die and give them one face. The risen Son of David is preached to Jews and Gentiles as the sure blessing, Acts 13:34, and the word of the cross goes out to nations that did not know God and run to Him, Isaiah 55:5. Pentecost is the first great harvest from that word, and the church's mission is the continuing rain that does not return empty.

The ending is already visible in the chapter. The joy of verse 12 and the transformed ground of verse 13 point to a creation in which the curse is gone. The Bible finishes with a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and on either side of it a tree of life yielding fruit each month, Revelation 22:1-2. In that city the invitation is still open, and the one who is thirsty is still told to come. What began as a call to people far from home ends as a welcome to a home where they never go hungry again, and the garden the exiles lost is found, larger, in the new creation.

sermon.title: The Great Invitation: Come! Drink! Eat! Live!
sermon.why: Preached by John Piper on July 31, 1988 from Isaiah 55:1-3, opening a five-part series through the whole chapter, this message unpacks the free, urgent invitation to come and be satisfied in God rather than laboring for what does not satisfy.

quiz.q: What does the picture of buying wine and milk without money teach about salvation?

options.text: Salvation is offered freely because its cost has already been paid by another; it cannot be earned by human effort or wealth.
options.note: This matches the free grace of the gospel, Ephesians 2:8-9.

options.text: It teaches that literal wine and milk are the only true satisfaction.
options.note: The wine and milk are figures for the richest, most satisfying provision God gives, not literal beverages alone.

options.text: It means God requires no response at all from those who come.
options.note: Salvation's cost is entirely free, but coming, buying, listening, and seeking are still active responses called for throughout the chapter.

options.text: It shows that only the wealthy can receive God's blessings.
options.note: The invitation is explicitly for those without money, the opposite of wealth-based access.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Isaiah 55:3 in Acts 13:34?

options.text: He quotes the sure mercies of David as proof that Christ's resurrection fulfills God's everlasting covenant with David.
options.note: Paul's argument in Acts 13 ties this verse directly to the resurrection of Jesus.

options.text: He uses it to argue that David's line ended with the exile.
options.note: Paul argues the opposite, that God's promise to David continues and is fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: He never references Isaiah 55 in his sermons.
He applies it only to Gentile believers, excluding Jewish hearers.
options.note: The sermon does reach Gentile God-fearers present, but Acts 13 is addressed first to a Jewish synagogue audience, not exclusively Gentile.

quiz.q: What does verse 11 promise about God's word?

options.text: It will never return to Him empty; it will always accomplish what He intends and prosper where He sends it.
options.note: The rain and snow image in verses 10-11 illustrates the certain effectiveness of God's spoken word.

options.text: It sometimes fails to accomplish its purpose.
options.note: The verse explicitly denies this; the word never returns empty.

options.text: It refers only to written Scripture, not spoken proclamation.
options.note: Written Scripture is included, but the image of rain and snow suggests active, sent-out speech, encompassing spoken proclamation as well.

options.text: It means God's word changes depending on human approval.
options.note: The word's success is independent of human approval; it accomplishes what God pleases.

quiz.q: What is the point of contrasting God's thoughts and ways with ours in verses 8-9?

options.text: God's mercy toward the wicked who return to Him will always exceed human expectation or logic.
options.note: This follows directly from verse 7's promise that God will freely pardon.

options.text: It teaches that human reasoning and God's reasoning are basically identical.
options.note: The verses explicitly say the opposite, God's ways are higher.

options.text: It means humans can never understand anything about God.
options.note: God's ways do exceed ours, but the passage still calls people to seek, listen, and understand; it is not total unknowability.

options.text: It refers only to differences in language and vocabulary.
options.note: It is about moral and redemptive logic, mercy exceeding expectation, not vocabulary.

questions: The invitation is to those who are thirsty and have no money. What are you laboring for right now that does not satisfy, and what would it look like to stop and simply come?
Verse 6 says seek the LORD while He may be found. Is there an urgency to your own pursuit of God, or have you let it drift into someday?
Verse 7 promises God will freely pardon those who forsake their own way and return to Him. What way of your own do you need to forsake this week?
God's thoughts are higher than our thoughts, especially in mercy. Where have you assumed God's forgiveness has limits that His own word does not actually place on it?
The chapter ends with thorns replaced by cypress, briers by myrtle, a picture of transformed landscape. What area of your life feels thorny right now that you can trust God's word to transform?

translationNotes.note: Sure mercies of David, chasdei David, is quoted in the Greek Old Testament and directly by Paul in Acts 13:34 as ta hosia Dauid, the holy and sure things of David, linking the phrase to Christ's resurrection.
Without money and without cost intensifies the same idea twice in Hebrew for emphasis; the invitation is doubly free, not merely discounted.
